title: The garden, fully told (Confessions 8)
hookLine: weeping under a fig tree, he hears take and read and opens Romans 13

cards: The garden of the house where Augustine is staying in Milan. Two friends have gone out there to get away from people: Augustine and his friend Alypius. Augustine is in pieces.
He has heard the sermons. He has run out of arguments. What's left, he says, is his own will, split in two, wanting God and wanting his old life, both at once.
He gets up, leaves Alypius sitting with a book of Paul's letters, goes off alone, and throws himself down under a fig tree. And he cries.

teach.b: Augustine gives us his own words from under that tree, in the Latin of the Confessions: quamdiu, quamdiu, cras et cras? How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow?
Why not now? Why not an end to it this very hour? Then he hears a voice from a house nearby, like a boy's or a girl's, chanting over and over: tolle lege, tolle lege.

teach.h: A CHILD'S VOICE: TAKE AND READ.
teach.b: Take and read, take and read. He stops crying long enough to think. Is this some children's game?
He can't remember any game with those words. So he takes it as a command: open the book, and read the first passage you find.
He remembers what he'd been told: how Anthony of the desert walked into church, heard a Gospel being read, and took it as spoken straight to him.

teach.h: THE FIRST PASSAGE HIS EYES FELL ON.
teach.b: So Augustine goes back to where Alypius is sitting, picks up the book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads in silence the first passage his eyes fall on. It's Romans thirteen.
Not in rioting and drunkenness, it says, not in impurity, not in quarreling. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He read no further, and didn't need to.
It was as if light flooded his heart and the darkness of doubt ran off. He marks the place with his finger and tells Alypius.
Alypius asks to see, reads the next line, about receiving the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself.

teach.h: PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: Then the two of them go straight inside to tell Monica. Augustine says she was overjoyed. Her tears had been answered.

how: Catholics read scripture at Mass, where the readings follow a set cycle, and on their own; lectio divina, a slow, prayerful reading of a short passage, is one way the Church encourages people to read it.

games.q: you're Augustine, in tears under a fig tree. from a house nearby, a child's voice keeps chanting: take and read. what do you do?
o: ignore it; children chant all sorts of things.
go back, open the book of Paul's letters, and read the first passage you see.
go next door and ask what game it is.
games.why: remembering Anthony, he took it as a command, opened to Romans 13, and read: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ.

practice: If you have a Bible or a Bible app, open it anywhere and read the first verse your eyes fall on, slowly, twice; if not, use a line you already know by heart.
Don't force it to mean something: if it speaks, let it, and if it doesn't, just stay with the words.
